y-m-22-01.title: Why the same scores can look like different shapes
y-m-22-01.topic: Frequency tables and histograms: shapes that look different depending on class width
y-m-22-01.goal: Confirm that organizing the same data with only a different class width can make the shape of the distribution look different, and say which part of your first judgment to keep and which part to fix when a new table and new information come in. Choose a class width for a presentation, with reasons.
y-m-22-01.material: 24 students in a class took a word test (out of 100, scores are integers). The teacher wants to organize the same scores while changing only the class width. All classes are read as 'at least ○ points and less than ○ points' (for example, '60 points or more and less than 80 points' includes 60 points and does not include 80 points). No individual names are used. The highest score is 98 points and the lowest score is 47 points.
y-m-22-01.thinking.0: Notice the limits of a judgment made from one table
y-m-22-01.thinking.1: Separate the part of a judgment to keep from the part to fix when new information comes in
y-m-22-01.thinking.2: Tell apart what the data confirms from guesses about causes
y-m-22-01.thinking.3: Compare and choose an organizing method that suits the purpose of a presentation
y-m-22-01.prereq.0: Reading classes and frequencies in a frequency table (the meaning of 'at least ○ and less than ○')
y-m-22-01.prereq.1: A histogram shows a frequency table with bars
y-m-22-01.prereq.2: Terms at the level of the Grade 7 data organization unit (class, frequency)
y-m-22-01.s.s1.prompt: The tables are revealed one at a time. Each time, choose your current judgment about the 'shape of the score distribution', and when the next table or information comes out, decide whether to keep or fix that judgment.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each table, point out in order which class has the greatest frequency and whether there is a place where the frequency drops compared with neighboring classes.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write down your judgment from the previous table in one sentence, and after seeing the new table, mark which part of that sentence stays the same and which part changes.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.info: [Class width 20 points] 40 points or more and less than 60 points: 5 students / 60 points or more and less than 80 points: 8 students / 80 points or more and less than 100 points: 11 students / Total 24 students
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: Looking at only this table, how would you judge the shape of the score distribution? (There can be more than one reasonable judgment.)
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.after: With three cells in the table you can say 'more students are on the high side', but you can't see how the frequency goes up and down inside a cell. We organized the same data again with a smaller class width.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The number of students increases toward higher scores, so it is a single-lump shape with the most students on the high-score side
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You haven't yet considered that with three cells in the table, you might not see how the frequency goes up and down between cells.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Most students are crowded on the low-score side and the number decreases toward the high side
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Read the table again to see which class has the greatest frequency. Which classes do 5, 8, and 11 students belong to?
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The number of students in the three classes is 5, 8, and 11, all around ten, so students are spread almost evenly
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: 5 and 11 differ by more than double. Think about what your standard is for seeing them as 'almost the same'.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: There are only three cells, so it's hard to be sure about the shape, and all you can say is that 11 students at 80 points or more is the most
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You were careful to say only what the table can show. This careful judgment is also reasonable at this step.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.info: [Class width 10 points] 40 points or more and less than 50 points: 1 student / 50 points or more and less than 60 points: 4 students / 60 points or more and less than 70 points: 6 students / 70 points or more and less than 80 points: 2 students / 80 points or more and less than 90 points: 6 students / 90 points or more and less than 100 points: 5 students / Total 24 students
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: How does it look when you see the scores of the same 24 students at 10-point intervals? Choose the thought that best fits your earlier judgment.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.after: The dip in the 70s, which was hidden at 20-point intervals, appeared at 10-point intervals. Even with the same data, the shape can look different depending on how the cells are divided.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Even with the same data, the shape you see can change depending on how the cells are divided. Look again at which cell in the earlier table you compared the frequency of the 70s with.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Comparing one class at a time and comparing the combined 80-and-above are different comparisons. Count how many students there are in total at 80 points or more.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The statement that there are many at 80 and above stays, but the statement that it is a single lump has to be fixed because the 70s dip
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You kept the part that says the high side has more and fixed only the part about the shape.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The table only tells the number of students. The cause that the problems were hard cannot be confirmed from this table.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.info: The teacher told you: "These 24 students are two class groups of 12 each. The scores of Group 갑 ranged from 47 to 72, and the scores of Group 을 ranged from 76 to 98."
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Based on this information, what do you think about why the 70s dip? (There can be more than one reasonable thought.)
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.after: The group information gives a candidate explanation that 'two lumps were joined together'. But a cause such as study method cannot be asserted from this data alone.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Group 을 scored higher because its study method is better, so if Group 갑 studies the same way, its scores will go up a lot
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The fact that the score ranges of the two groups are different does not tell you whether study method is the cause. You also don't know whether their original ability or preparation time was the same.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The score ranges of the two groups hardly overlap, so it may be a shape where two lumps are joined. It would be clearer to organize them separately by group
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You connected the information the data has (groups, score ranges) with the shape.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The group information has nothing to do with the shape, and the dip is a coincidence
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The information that the two groups hardly overlap can be connected to the dip. Before saying there is no relationship, think about how the score ranges of the two groups are reflected in the shape.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Each group has only 12 students, so it's even harder to describe the shape if drawn separately. Still, it's worth noting that the score ranges don't overlap
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You also considered the limits when the number of data values is small. This careful judgment is also reasonable.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.reflect: Even the same data looked like different shapes depending on class width, and each time new information came in, one part of the judgment was kept (more on the high side) and another part was fixed (a single lump). Say at which step you changed which part of your judgment and what part you did not change. Also point out that the group information is an 'explanation of the shape' but not a 'proof of the cause'.
y-m-22-01.s.s2.prompt: Suppose you put the scores of these 24 students as a histogram in a notice to parents. What class width would you use? Write the reason you chose it, together with the shape of the distribution you can see at that class width. (There is more than one right answer.)
y-m-22-01.s.s2.hint.0: First choose a class width and reread the closest of the tables you saw earlier.
y-m-22-01.s.s2.hint.1: In that table, find whether there is a class with the greatest frequency and a class that dips, and write it in one sentence.
y-m-22-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say what shape the class width you chose shows and what shape it hides?
y-m-22-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can the sentences you wrote about the 'shape' be confirmed with the frequencies (numbers) in the table?
y-m-22-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Do you know why you could choose another class width, and did you write both the good points and the drawbacks of your choice?
y-m-22-01.s.s2.model.0: I'll use 10-point intervals. At 20-point intervals it looks like only a single lump that increases toward higher scores, but if I divide it into 10 points, the dip in the 70s shows up, and you can see that the scores are split into two groups.
y-m-22-01.s.s2.model.1: You could also try 5-point intervals, but for 24 students there would be too many cells and the frequencies would look uneven. I'll choose 10 points and also say the shape that there are few in the 70s and many crowded in the 60s and 80s. It's also easy to read because there are 6 cells.
y-m-22-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that compares with other sizes and gives advantages and disadvantages.
y-m-22-01.s.s2.model.2: I'll group by 20 points to convey at a glance that 'overall, more students are on the high-score side'. However, the dip in the 70s is hidden, so I'll include the 10-point interval table next to it.
y-m-22-01.s.s2.modelNote.2: An answer that knows the limits and offers a remedy.
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Keep both the statement that there are many at 80 and above and the statement that they are in one lump. We only split the interval, and it is the same data, so the judgment does not change at all
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The first statement that there are many at 80 and above is now wrong, so discard it entirely. Because the 60s and the 80s both have the same 6 students
y-m-22-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Keep the statement that there are many at 80 and above, and add that the dip in the 70s is because the problems in that interval were unusually hard

y-m-22-02.title: Finding the wrong line in a reading-time solution
y-m-22-02.topic: Estimating the mean from a frequency table: fixing the wrong line in a solution
y-m-22-02.goal: Find and fix the wrong line in a solution that estimates the mean using class midpoints from a frequency table, and build the habit of recognizing that the obtained value is an estimate and checking whether its size is within the range of the data.
y-m-22-02.material:
The time (minutes) that 20 students read books in a day is organized in a frequency table. Each class is 'at least ○ minutes and less than ○ minutes'.
[Frequency table] 0 minutes or more and less than 20 minutes: 3 students / 20 minutes or more and less than 40 minutes: 5 students / 40 minutes or more and less than 60 minutes: 8 students / 60 minutes or more and less than 80 minutes: 4 students / Total 20 students
A frequency table does not have each student's exact time, so we estimate the mean by assuming that every student in a class read for the midpoint of that class (the class mark). Below is one student's solution.
y-m-22-02.thinking.0: Find the error by considering what each line of the solution is a quantity of
y-m-22-02.thinking.1: Check the reasonableness of whether the result fits the range of the data
y-m-22-02.thinking.2: Explain why a difference arises between the estimated value and the actual value
y-m-22-02.prereq.0: Reading classes and frequencies in a frequency table
y-m-22-02.prereq.1: What the midpoint of a class (class mark) is
y-m-22-02.prereq.2: The meaning of mean (the total divided by the number of values)
y-m-22-02.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, write down whether the number that came out stands for 'number of students' or 'sum of time'.
y-m-22-02.s.s1.line.0: The class mark is the midpoint of each class, so it is 10 minutes, 30 minutes, 50 minutes, 70 minutes.
y-m-22-02.s.s1.line.1: Multiplying each class mark by the frequency of that class gives 30, 150, 400, 280.
y-m-22-02.s.s1.line.2: Adding all four of these values gives 860.
y-m-22-02.s.s1.line.3: There are 4 classes, so dividing 860 by 4 gives a mean of about 215 minutes.
y-m-22-02.s.s1.line.4: So one student reads about 215 minutes a day on average.
y-m-22-02.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong where it divides 860 by the number of classes (4). 860 is the sum of the estimated reading times of all 20 students, so it must be divided by the number of students, 20. Line 5 simply uses the result of line 4, so it is wrong too. 215 minutes is even greater than 80 minutes, the end of the longest class, so you can tell it cannot be the mean even before finishing the calculation.
y-m-22-02.s.s2.prompt: After fixing the wrong line, what is the estimated mean?
y-m-22-02.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether the fixed value is between 0 minutes and 80 minutes and near the class mark of the class with a large frequency.
y-m-22-02.s.s2.o.a: About 40 minutes (the mean of the four class marks)
y-m-22-02.s.s2.r.a: You averaged only the class marks and ignored the frequencies. This counts classes with many students and classes with few students the same.
y-m-22-02.s.s2.o.b: About 50 minutes (the class mark of the class with the greatest frequency)
y-m-22-02.s.s2.r.b: You mistook the value of the class with the most students for the mean. The mean reflects the values of all students.
y-m-22-02.s.s2.explain: 860÷20=43, so it is about 43 minutes. A mean using class marks is an estimated value.
y-m-22-02.s.s3.hint.0: Choose one class and think about whether the times the students in it read really are all the midpoint.
y-m-22-02.s.s3.hint.1: Write separately the information that is in the table and the information that is not, and consider how the missing information would affect the mean.
y-m-22-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: I think it's exactly the same / it could be different ... because ...
y-m-22-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write that this value rests on 'seeing every student in a class as having read for the midpoint'?
y-m-22-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say separately that it could be the same and could be different?
y-m-22-02.s.s3.model.0: It can't be said to be exactly the same. A frequency table does not have the exact time each student read, so it is a value estimated by assuming everyone read for the midpoint of their class. For example, in the class 40 minutes or more and less than 60 minutes, most of them may actually have read about 41 minutes.
y-m-22-02.s.s3.model.1: It can differ from the actual mean. Within the same class the reading times are different from each other, so changing them to the class mark causes an error. However, if students who read less than the midpoint and students who read more are mixed about equally within a class, they offset each other and it could be almost the same.
y-m-22-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that also mentions the case where they could be the same.
y-m-22-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in this solution.
y-m-22-02.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether the result in each line is a value within the range where the data in this table lies.
y-m-22-02.s.s2.hint.1: Write down for each choice 'what was divided by what,' and compare the relationship between it and the result of line 3 of the solution.
y-m-22-02.s.s2.o.c: About 43 minutes (860 divided by the number of students)
y-m-22-02.s.s2.r.c: The corrected value is within the range of the data.
y-m-22-02.s.s2.o.d: About 215 minutes (the solution as it is)
y-m-22-02.s.s2.r.d: You did not check whether the value goes outside the range of the data.
y-m-22-02.s.s3.prompt: Can we say the average estimated by this method is exactly equal to the average of the times the 20 students actually read? Write your reason.

y-m-22-03.title: Sorting out what is certain in a stem-and-leaf plot
y-m-22-03.topic: Stem-and-leaf plots: what can and cannot be said for certain from the plot
y-m-22-03.goal: Read a stem-and-leaf plot and tell apart what can be said for certain from the plot, what applies the reading method wrongly, and guesses about causes that cannot be known from the data alone. Check which values change and which stay the same when one more data value is added.
y-m-22-03.material:
The number of sit-ups that 15 students did in 1 minute is shown in a stem-and-leaf plot. The stem is the tens digit and the leaf is the ones digit, and '1 | 2' means 12 times. Leaves are written from the smallest number.
Stem | Leaf
1 | 2 5 8
2 | 0 1 3 4 4 7
3 | 1 2 5 6
4 | 0 8
(Read aloud, you read each row, like 'stem 1, leaves 2, 5, 8', 'stem 2, leaves 0, 1, 3, 4, 4, 7'.)
y-m-22-03.thinking.0: Separate the evidence the plot gives from guesses
y-m-22-03.thinking.1: Check whether the rule for reading the plot was applied correctly
y-m-22-03.thinking.2: Check which judgments change when information changes
y-m-22-03.prereq.0: How to read a stem-and-leaf plot (the stem is the tens digit, the leaf is the ones digit)
y-m-22-03.prereq.1: The meanings of minimum, maximum, and mode
y-m-22-03.prereq.2: The meaning of median (when the number of data values is odd and when it is even)
y-m-22-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything that can be said for certain from this plot alone.
y-m-22-03.s.s1.hint.0: Divide each statement into whether it 'can be counted or read directly from the plot' and whether it is 'a statement with a reason added'.
y-m-22-03.s.s1.hint.1: First count and write down the number of leaves for each stem, and match them with the statements one at a time.
y-m-22-03.s.s1.o.a: More students did 40 or more than students in the 30s
y-m-22-03.s.s1.r.a: Count how many leaves stem 4 and stem 3 each have and compare.
y-m-22-03.s.s1.o.b: The 20s stem has 6 leaves, so the 20s have the most students
y-m-22-03.s.s1.r.b: You applied correctly the reading that the number of leaves in each stem is the number of students in that row.
y-m-22-03.s.s1.o.c: The leaf 5 on stem 3 means 3 plus 5, which is 8 times
y-m-22-03.s.s1.r.c: Check again the reading rule that the stem is the tens digit and the leaf is the ones digit.
y-m-22-03.s.s1.o.d: 24 is the only value with the same number of times appearing twice
y-m-22-03.s.s1.r.d: You found and read the place where the same leaf repeated in one row.
y-m-22-03.s.s1.o.e: The 20s have the most because they practiced sit-ups a lot
y-m-22-03.s.s1.r.e: The plot only tells the number of times. A cause such as whether they practiced cannot be confirmed from the plot.
y-m-22-03.s.s1.o.f: The difference between the number of times of the student who did the most and the student who did the fewest is 36
y-m-22-03.s.s1.r.f: You read the minimum and maximum from the first leaf of the top row and the last leaf of the bottom row.
y-m-22-03.s.s1.explain: What can be said for certain from the plot is b, d, f. a is backwards, since there are 2 students in the 40s and 4 in the 30s. c applies the reading rule wrongly (it is 35 times), and e is a guess about a cause that cannot be known from the plot alone.
y-m-22-03.s.s2.prompt: If you change this plot into a frequency table with 10-time intervals ('10 times or more and less than 20 times', etc.), what information disappears?
y-m-22-03.s.s2.hint.0: Read the leaves of the 20s row in the plot one by one, then compare them with what can be read from one cell of the table, '20 times or more and less than 30 times: 6 students'.
y-m-22-03.s.s2.hint.1: Find what fact can be read from the plot but cannot be read from the table.
y-m-22-03.s.s2.o.a: The fact that the 20s have 6 students, the most among the stems
y-m-22-03.s.s2.r.a: The frequency for 20 times or more and less than 30 times also remains in the table. Find which cell of the table you can read it from.
y-m-22-03.s.s2.o.b: The fact that 24 appears twice within the 20s
y-m-22-03.s.s2.o.c: The fact itself that there are more students in the 20s than in the 30s
y-m-22-03.s.s2.r.c: You can also compare the frequencies of the two classes in the table. Say which cell and which cell.
y-m-22-03.s.s2.o.d: The fact that the total number of students who took part in the survey is 15
y-m-22-03.s.s2.r.d: The total of the frequencies remains in the table too. Think about how you check the total in the table.
y-m-22-03.s.s2.explain: A frequency table only tells the number of students in each class, so individual values within the same class (24 appearing twice) cannot be seen. A stem-and-leaf plot keeps the original values as they are.
y-m-22-03.s.s3.prompt: One more student joined later and did 50 times. A leaf 0 is added to stem 5, making 16 students in all. (With 15 students, the median was the 8th value, 24 times.) Of 'the 20s have the most', '24 is a value that appeared twice', and the median that you read earlier, write which changes and which stays the same, and how you checked.
y-m-22-03.s.s3.hint.0: Count the 16 values from the smallest and write down which positions the middle values are in.
y-m-22-03.s.s3.hint.1: Count the number of leaves in the 20s row and the number of times 24 appears, before and after adding the new leaf, and compare them.
y-m-22-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The median changes to ... ... stays the same. The way I checked was ...
y-m-22-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you find the median reflecting that with 16 students there are two middle values, not one?
y-m-22-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check why 'the number of students in the 20s' and '24 appearing twice' do not change even when a new student is added?
y-m-22-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write how you checked (counted in order, reread the rows, etc.)?
y-m-22-03.s.s3.model.0: With 16 students, the median changes to 25.5 times, which is between the 8th value, 24, and the 9th value, 27. The 20s having the most with 6 students and 24 appearing twice stay the same. This is because only one leaf was added to stem 5.
y-m-22-03.s.s3.model.1: I counted in order and the 8th is 24 and the 9th is 27, so the median becomes 25.5 times and went up a little. The number of students in the 20s (6) doesn't change and 24 appearing twice is the same too, so those stay.
y-m-22-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that states the way of checking as counting in order.

y-m-22-04.title: What can be said from the commute-time table and what more we need to know
y-m-22-04.topic: What a frequency table can and cannot tell (sufficiency of information)
y-m-22-04.goal: Separate statements the frequency table guarantees from statements it does not, and say what information outside the table is needed to answer a certain question.
y-m-22-04.material:
The commute times (minutes) of 30 students are organized in a frequency table. Each class is 'at least ○ minutes and less than ○ minutes'. The commute-time data of individual students is not kept, and only this table remains.
Commute time / Number of students
0 minutes or more and less than 10 minutes / 4 students
10 minutes or more and less than 20 minutes / 9 students
20 minutes or more and less than 30 minutes / 11 students
30 minutes or more and less than 40 minutes / 5 students
40 minutes or more and less than 50 minutes / 1 student
Total 30 students
(Read aloud, you read one row at a time, like '0 minutes or more and less than 10 minutes, 4 students'.)
y-m-22-04.thinking.0: Separate what the table guarantees from what it does not
y-m-22-04.thinking.1: Decide whether the information is enough to draw a conclusion
y-m-22-04.thinking.2: State specifically what extra information is needed
y-m-22-04.prereq.0: Reading classes and frequencies in a frequency table
y-m-22-04.prereq.1: The meaning of median (the middle value when placed in order)
y-m-22-04.prereq.2: Being able to guess the difference between when part of the data was sampled and when everyone was surveyed
y-m-22-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything that can be said for certain from this table alone.
y-m-22-04.s.s1.hint.0: Divide each statement into whether it is about 'the number of students in a whole class' or about 'a specific value within a class'.
y-m-22-04.s.s1.hint.1: Add the frequencies in order from the smallest class and find which class the 15th and 16th students are in.
y-m-22-04.s.s1.o.a: There are 24 students whose commute time is less than 30 minutes
y-m-22-04.s.s1.r.a: This is a fact confirmed from the table by adding the frequencies of several classes.
y-m-22-04.s.s1.o.b: Among the students in 20 minutes or more and less than 30 minutes, there is at least one student whose trip takes exactly 25 minutes
y-m-22-04.s.s1.r.b: There being 11 students in 20 minutes or more and less than 30 minutes is different from there being a student of 25 minutes. Does the table tell the values inside this cell?
y-m-22-04.s.s1.o.c: 20 minutes or more and less than 30 minutes has the most, 11 students
y-m-22-04.s.s1.r.c: This is a fact from reading the class with the greatest frequency.
y-m-22-04.s.s1.o.d: The student with the longest commute time belongs to 40 minutes or more and less than 50 minutes and takes exactly 45 minutes
y-m-22-04.s.s1.r.d: There being 1 student in 40 minutes or more and less than 50 minutes is not the same as that student being 45 minutes. Does the table tell the values inside this cell?
y-m-22-04.s.s1.o.e: If you line up the 30 students in order of commute time, the student in the middle belongs to a class in the 20s of minutes
y-m-22-04.s.s1.r.e: This is a fact from reading the class that contains the median using the frequencies accumulated in order.
y-m-22-04.s.s1.o.f: The mean that reflects the commute times of all 30 students is exactly 22 minutes
y-m-22-04.s.s1.r.f: The table does not have each student's exact time. Think about whether the mean can be found exactly.
y-m-22-04.s.s1.explain: a (4+9+11=24), c (11 students is the most), and e (the 15th and 16th students are both in 20 minutes or more and less than 30 minutes) are certain from the table. b and d talk about specific values within a class, and f talks about the exact mean, which cannot be known from the table alone (using class marks you can estimate about 21.7 minutes, but it is not exact).
y-m-22-04.s.s2.prompt: To answer 'How many students have a commute time of 25 minutes or more?', what else would you need besides the table?
y-m-22-04.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether 25 minutes is the same as a class boundary in the table, and which class it is inside.
y-m-22-04.s.s2.hint.1: Work out separately the fewest and the most students there could be with 25 minutes or more.
y-m-22-04.s.s2.o.a: Among the 11 students of the 20s class, the number with 25 minutes or more
y-m-22-04.s.s2.r.a: This is information about the position within a class, which the table does not tell.
y-m-22-04.s.s2.o.b: A number that tells how many students are in the 30 minutes or more and less than 40 minutes class
y-m-22-04.s.s2.r.b: That frequency (5 students) is already in the table. Which class is the boundary that separates 25 minutes and above inside?
y-m-22-04.s.s2.o.c: A number that tells what the mean commute time of the 30 students is in minutes
y-m-22-04.s.s2.r.c: A single mean cannot tell whether the students inside the 20s class are above or below 25 minutes.
y-m-22-04.s.s2.o.d: A number that tells how many students in total are organized in the table
y-m-22-04.s.s2.r.d: The total number of students (30) is already in the table. Look at whether the boundary of 25 minutes matches a class boundary.
y-m-22-04.s.s2.explain: 25 minutes is inside the class 20 minutes or more and less than 30 minutes, so you need to know how many of this class's 11 students are 25 minutes or more. 30 minutes or more (6 students) can be known from the table, but for 25 minutes or more the table alone can only say a range of at least 6 students and at most 17 students.
y-m-22-04.s.s3.prompt: Jaemin said, "6 students take 30 minutes or more, which is one fifth of all 30, so the students at this school have rather short commute times." Write separately the part of this statement that is confirmed by the table and what you would need to know more to state this conclusion.
y-m-22-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write Jaemin's statement in two sentences: 'the part confirmed by numbers' and 'the interpretation that it is short'.
y-m-22-04.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what you must compare with to say 'short', and how not knowing who these 30 are would affect the conclusion.
y-m-22-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: What the table confirms is ... What I need to know more is ...
y-m-22-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you tell apart that '6 students, one fifth' is a fact confirmed by the table and 'rather short' is an interpretation?
y-m-22-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write specifically the information needed to say 'short' (a standard, something to compare with, what kind of students these 30 are)?
y-m-22-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid insisting Jaemin's statement is wrong and also say how far it is right?
y-m-22-04.s.s3.model.0: Looking at the table, it is true that 6 students take 30 minutes or more, which is one fifth of 30. But to say 'rather short', you need a standard for from how many minutes counts as long, and you also need data to compare with other schools or last year. Also, we can't tell whether these 30 students represent the whole school.
y-m-22-04.s.s3.model.1: That it is 6 students and one fifth can be known from the table. But 20 minutes or more is also 17 students, more than half, so it may be hard to just say short. To judge whether it is short, I need a standard to compare with.
y-m-22-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that checked the conclusion by finding another number (17 students) in the same table.

y-m-22-05.topic: Mean and frequency distribution: even with the same mean, the class with the most can be different
y-m-22-05.material:
20 students took a math quiz. Each score belongs to one of 50 points or more and less than 60 points, 60 points or more and less than 70 points, 70 points or more and less than 80 points, and 80 points or more and less than 90 points, and the class marks of the four classes are 55 points, 65 points, 75 points, 85 points. The mean is estimated by assuming that every student in a class got the class mark.
Sujeong said, "If the mean is 70 points, the 70s will have the most students."
y-m-22-05.thinking.0: Test with a counterexample whether a generalization always holds
y-m-22-05.thinking.1: Make a table yourself that meets several conditions at the same time
y-m-22-05.thinking.2: Explain where the mean sits in a distribution
y-m-22-05.prereq.0: Reading classes and frequencies in a frequency table
y-m-22-05.prereq.1: How to estimate the mean using class marks (the midpoints of classes)
y-m-22-05.s.s1.prompt: How do you judge Sujeong's statement?
y-m-22-05.s.s1.hint.0: Think about how scores lower than 70 and scores higher than 70 must balance for the mean to be 70 points.
y-m-22-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write one way to divide the 20 students among the four classes and estimate what the mean would be.
y-m-22-05.s.s1.explain: The mean is not the place with many students, but is closer to the balance point of all the scores. Even when students are split between the low side and the high side, the mean can be 70 points. Let's make one and check it ourselves.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.hint.0: First write four numbers whose sum of students is 20, multiply by the class marks, add them, and check whether you get 1400.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how the students on the lower-score side and the higher side must be matched for the mean to be 70, and work out how to change the other classes when you change the number of students in one class.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.ok.c1: Every class has at least one student.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Every class must have at least one student.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The numbers of students are natural numbers.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The numbers of students must be natural numbers.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The numbers of students in the four classes must add up to 20.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.ok.c4: The mean estimated with class marks is 70 points.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.fail.c4: The sum of class mark × number of students is not 1400 (= 70 × 20). The mean is not 70 points.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.ok.c5: The 70s is not the class with the most.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.fail.c5: The 70s is the class with the most (or tied for first). There must be another class with more students than the 70s.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.explain: For example, (4, 8, 2, 6) gives 55×4+65×8+75×2+85×6=220+520+150+510=1400, with 20 students and a mean of 70 points, but the 70s has 2 students, the fewest. (5, 6, 3, 6), (8, 2, 2, 8) and so on also work. If the low side and the high side balance, the mean becomes 70 points.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the tables you made, and explain, using the numbers in that table, why the 70s does not have the most students even though the mean is 70 points.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Choose one table you made and write how much lower and higher each class is than the mean of 70 points.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write in one sentence how the students on the low side and on the high side balance the mean to 70 points.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: In the table you chose, did you say how the low-score side and the high-score side balance the mean?
y-m-22-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you show with the numbers of your table that 'the mean is not where the most students are'?
y-m-22-05.s.s2.because.model.0: With (4, 8, 2, 6), the 4 students in the 50s make low scores and the 6 students in the 80s make high scores, and the two sides balance each other, so the mean becomes 70 points. Yet there are only 2 students in the 70s.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.because.model.1: The mean is not a value that tells where there are many students; it is the value you get when all the scores are gathered and divided evenly. In (5, 6, 3, 6), students are split between the low side and the high side, like 6 students in the 60s and 6 in the 80s, and even though the 70s has only 3, the mean is 70 points.
y-m-22-05.title: Making Frequency Tables with the Same Mean Yourself
y-m-22-05.goal: Test whether the idea 'if the mean is some value, the class near that value has the most' always holds by making frequency tables that fit the conditions yourself, and explain the relationship between the mean and the class with the most students.
y-m-22-05.s.s1.o.a: In a frequency table whose mean is 70, the 70s always have the fewest students
y-m-22-05.s.s1.r.a: You are asserting the opposite direction. Test whether this is always so too.
y-m-22-05.s.s1.o.b: In a frequency table whose mean is 70, the number of students below 70 and the number of students 70 and above are always equal
y-m-22-05.s.s1.r.b: You thought of the mean like the middle value (median). Think about whether the mean and the middle value are the same.
y-m-22-05.s.s1.o.c: Among frequency tables whose mean is 70, there are some in which the 70s do not have the most students
y-m-22-05.s.s1.o.d: In a frequency table whose mean is 70, the 70s always have the most students
y-m-22-05.s.s1.r.d: You believe the most students are where the mean is. Think about whether there is only one way for the mean to be 70.
y-m-22-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different frequency tables that fit the conditions. (f1: number of students in the 50s, f2: the 60s, f3: the 70s, f4: the 80s) All 20 students must be in one of the four classes, each class must have at least one student, the estimated mean must be exactly 70, and there must be at least one class with more students than the 70s.

y-m-22-06.title: Different ways to divide jump-rope records into five classes
y-m-22-06.topic: Making a frequency table: choosing the starting value and size of the classes to fit conditions
y-m-22-06.goal: Choose the starting value and size of the classes in several ways under the conditions that all records fit, no class is empty, and no class is overloaded; handle the boundary ('less than') correctly; and compare how the distribution looks different depending on the design.
y-m-22-06.material:
The numbers of jump-rope jumps (times, integers) that 16 students did in 1 minute, listed from the smallest, are as follows.
8, 12, 15, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28, 31, 34, 37, 41, 55
These records are organized in a frequency table. There are five classes, all the same size, written as 'at least ○ times and less than ○ times'. The first class starts at a times or more and the class width is w times (a is a natural number 0 or more, w is a natural number 1 or more). That is, the classes go in order: a or more and less than a+w, a+w or more and less than a+2w, … The following conditions must be kept. ① The records of all 16 students fall within the five classes ② No class is empty ③ No class has more than 8 students (half of the total).
y-m-22-06.thinking.1: Apply class boundaries ('at least / less than') exactly
y-m-22-06.thinking.2: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of a design
y-m-22-06.prereq.0: Reading classes and frequencies in a frequency table
y-m-22-06.prereq.1: The meaning of 'at least ○ and less than ○'
y-m-22-06.prereq.2: The rule of making class widths equal
y-m-22-06.s.s1.hint.0: Find which class the smallest record and the largest record each fall into.
y-m-22-06.s.s1.o.c: The record of 55 times does not fit into any class
y-m-22-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 designs of classes that keep all of the conditions ①②③ with different class widths w.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a class width, and first check whether the end of the last class (a+5w) is greater than 55.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.hint.1: Count the records that fall in each class one by one, and if any class is empty or has more than 8, change the starting value or width and count again.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.var.a: Starting value of the first class a (times)
y-m-22-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The starting value and class width are natural numbers.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The starting value a must be a natural number 0 or more and the class width w must be a natural number 1 or more.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The records of all 16 students fall within the five classes.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The smallest record 8 times or the largest record 55 times is outside the five classes. The last class is 'less than', so its upper end is not included.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The number of students in the 1st class is 1 or more and 8 or fewer.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The 1st class has 0 students or more than 8. Try changing the class width or the starting value.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.ok.c4: The number of students in the 2nd class is 1 or more and 8 or fewer.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.fail.c4: The 2nd class has 0 students or more than 8. Try changing the class width or the starting value.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.ok.c5: The number of students in the 3rd class is 1 or more and 8 or fewer.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.fail.c5: The 3rd class has 0 students or more than 8. Try changing the class width or the starting value.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.ok.c6: The number of students in the 4th class is 1 or more and 8 or fewer.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.fail.c6: The 4th class has 0 students or more than 8. Try changing the class width or the starting value.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.ok.c7: The number of students in the 5th class is 1 or more and 8 or fewer.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.fail.c7: The 5th class has 0 students or more than 8. Try changing the class width or the starting value.
y-m-22-06.s.s2.explain: For example, with a=8, w=10 the frequencies are 4, 6, 4, 1, 1 students, and with a=0, w=12 they are 1, 7, 5, 2, 1 students. a=5, w=10 leaves out 55 times, and a=0, w=20 has the fourth and fifth classes empty, so they don't fit the conditions.
y-m-22-06.s.s3.prompt: Choose one of the two designs you made, write how the distribution of jump-rope records looks in that design, and write at least one thing that this design shows well (or hides).
y-m-22-06.s.s3.hint.0: Choose one design you made and write the frequencies of the five classes in order.
y-m-22-06.s.s3.hint.1: In those frequencies, write one sentence each about the class with the most, the class with the fewest, and where the isolated record is.
y-m-22-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: With a=○, w=○, ... is large and ... can be seen. This design ...
y-m-22-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the sentence you wrote based on actually counting the frequencies of the design you chose?
y-m-22-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think about both what this design shows and what it hides?
y-m-22-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say how an isolated record like 55 times looks in this design?
y-m-22-06.s.s3.model.0: I used a=8, w=10. The 18 times or more and less than 28 times class has the most with 6 students, and the 38-or-more and 48-or-more classes have 1 student each, so the shape with a long tail stretching toward the high side shows up well.
y-m-22-06.s.s3.model.1: I made the class width 12 times and started at 0. 7 students gather in 12 times or more and less than 24 times, and the last class has only one record of 55 times by itself, so the record that is far off by itself stands out, which I thought was good.
y-m-22-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that talks about how the isolated record shows.
y-m-22-06.s.s1.prompt: Dongjun set the classes with a=5, w=10. That is, 5 or more and less than 15, 15 or more and less than 25, 25 or more and less than 35, 35 or more and less than 45, and 45 or more and less than 55. Why do these classes fail to meet condition ① (all 16 students' records fall within the five classes)?
y-m-22-06.s.s1.hint.1: Put the 16 records into classes one by one and check whether any record can't be put into any class.
y-m-22-06.s.s1.o.a: 8 is less than the first class (5 or more), so there is no class for it
y-m-22-06.s.s1.r.a: Check yourself whether 8 fits in 5 or more and less than 15.
y-m-22-06.s.s1.o.b: More than 8 students crowd into the class 15 or more and less than 25, so they can't all fit in the class
y-m-22-06.s.s1.r.b: Count the records that fall in that class yourself. Crowding is a problem for condition ③, and condition ① asks whether any records are left outside the classes.
y-m-22-06.s.s1.o.d: There are only five classes, so there are not enough classes for all 16 students' records
y-m-22-06.s.s1.r.d: Even with five classes, all the records can fit. Assign which record goes where yourself.
y-m-22-06.s.s1.explain: The last class is '45 or more and less than 55', so 55 cannot go in. So the last cell of this class may also be empty (this breaks condition ② too). a+5w=55 does not include 55, so a+5w must be greater than 55.
y-m-22-06.s.s3.model.2: I made the class width 11 and a=3. The frequencies are 2, 6, 5, 2, 1, which shows that 55 stands alone, apart from the rest.

y-m-22-07.title: Can we say 'twice as many' just from the bar heights?
y-m-22-07.topic: Reading histograms: how the start of the vertical axis affects comparing bar heights
y-m-22-07.goal: Notice that in a histogram whose vertical axis does not start at 0 the ratio of bar heights differs from the ratio of frequencies, judge the difference from the actual frequencies, and rewrite it as a notice that causes no misunderstanding.
y-m-22-07.thinking.0: Separate the evidence of a graph (height) from the actual value (frequency)
y-m-22-07.thinking.1: Check whether a claim comes from the evidence
y-m-22-07.thinking.2: Rewrite with numbers so readers don't misunderstand
y-m-22-07.prereq.0: Reading the horizontal axis (class) and vertical axis (frequency) of a histogram
y-m-22-07.prereq.1: Checking the total number of people with the sum of frequencies
y-m-22-07.prereq.2: Comparing two numbers by about how many times as large
y-m-22-07.s.s1.prompt: This is the process by which a reader checked whether the notice's text is right. Choose the line whose reasoning is wrong.
y-m-22-07.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine how the heights of the three bars would look different if the vertical axis started at 0.
y-m-22-07.s.s1.line.0: In the figure, the bar for 5 books or more and less than 10 books is the tallest.
y-m-22-07.s.s1.line.1: The height of a bar is proportional to the number of students, so the ratio of the visible heights is the ratio of the numbers of students.
y-m-22-07.s.s1.line.2: The height of the middle bar looks about 2 times the height of the first bar.
y-m-22-07.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the number of students in 5 books or more and less than 10 books is about 2 times the number in 0 books or more and less than 5 books.
y-m-22-07.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. If the vertical axis starts not at 0 but at 40 students, the visible height of a bar is a length corresponding to (frequency − 40), so it is not proportional to the number of students. The heights look like 6:12:4, but the actual numbers of students are 46:52:44. Line 4 is a conclusion that rests on line 2, so it is wrong too. Lines 1 and 3 record facts seen with the eyes in the figure.
y-m-22-07.s.s2.prompt: Using the actual numbers of students, about how many times the number of students in 0 books or more and less than 5 books (46 students) is the number in 5 books or more and less than 10 books (52 students)? (Estimate to one decimal place.)
y-m-22-07.s.s2.hint.0: Estimate how large the difference between the two numbers (52−46) is compared with 46.
y-m-22-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write how many students 2 times and 1.5 times 46 are, and compare them with 52.
y-m-22-07.s.s2.r.b: Check whether the difference between the numbers of students 52 and 46 (6 students) reaches half of 46.
y-m-22-07.s.s2.r.c: First check whether 52 is greater or less than 46.
y-m-22-07.s.s2.explain: 52÷46 is about 1.13, so about 1.1 times. The notice's 'about twice' was a value seen from the heights in the figure, and in reality the difference is not big.
y-m-22-07.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite the notice text so that parents will not misunderstand when they read it. You must use the numbers of students and truthfully say how large the differences among the three classes are.
y-m-22-07.s.s3.hint.0: First put the actual numbers of students 52, 46, 44 into the sentence, and write which is the greatest and by how much they differ.
y-m-22-07.s.s3.hint.1: Find the expressions in the original text that came from the heights in the figure and change them to the actual numbers.
y-m-22-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The number of students who borrowed 5 books or more and less than 10 books is ... which is ...
y-m-22-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Are the numbers in your rewritten text the same as the actual numbers of students?
y-m-22-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid expressions that came from the heights in the figure, like 'overwhelmingly' and 'twice'?
y-m-22-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you tell the reader that the vertical axis does not start at 0, or give the actual numbers?
y-m-22-07.s.s3.model.0: The students who borrowed 5 books or more and less than 10 books are the most with 52 students, but 0 books or more and less than 5 books has 46 students and 10 books or more and less than 15 books has 44, so the difference is not big. The vertical axis of the figure starts at 40 students, so the difference between the bars looks bigger.
y-m-22-07.s.s3.model.1: Out of 142 students, 52 borrowed 5 to 9 books, the most, and the other two classes were also similar with 46 and 44. In all three classes, students are fairly evenly spread.
y-m-22-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that compared with the whole of 142.
y-m-22-07.material:
A histogram was printed in the library notice. It divides 142 students into three classes by the number of books they borrowed in a month.
[The histogram described in words] The horizontal axis shows '0 or more and less than 5 books', '5 or more and less than 10 books', and '10 or more and less than 15 books'. The vertical axis is the number of students, with marks from bottom to top at 40, 44, 48, 52 students. Below the mark 40 is not drawn in the picture. The actual frequencies of the three bars are 46, 52, 44 students in order.
Notice text: "Overwhelmingly many students borrowed 5 or more and less than 10 books! It's about double the other classes."
y-m-22-07.s.s1.hint.0: Think with the marks about which part of the vertical axis the height of one bar measures from and to.
y-m-22-07.s.s2.r.a: You compared using the actual numbers of students.
y-m-22-07.s.s2.r.d: This is a value estimated from the bar heights in the picture. Remove the effect of the vertical axis starting at 40 and compare the actual numbers of students.
y-m-22-07.s.s3.model.2: 5 or more and less than 10 books has 52 students, 0 or more and less than 5 has 46, and 10 or more and less than 15 has 44, so the difference between the class with the most and the class with the fewest is 8 students.

y-m-22-08.title: Testing the statement 'about half the students are above the mean'
y-m-22-08.topic: Mean and distribution of data: the number of values above the mean
y-m-22-08.goal: Test by making counterexamples yourself whether the idea 'the numbers of values above and below the mean are almost the same' always holds, and explain why the mean and the median behave differently with respect to the number of upper values.
y-m-22-08.material: We talk about task scores (integers from 0 to 100) of 5 students. Mina said, "The students who got scores higher than the mean are always about half of everyone, and the other half got scores lower than the mean." The mean is the value you get by adding the scores of the 5 students and dividing by 5. A student whose score is equal to the mean is put on neither the 'higher' side nor the 'lower' side.
y-m-22-08.thinking.0: Test the claim 'always' with a counterexample
y-m-22-08.thinking.1: Explain how the mean is pulled by extreme values
y-m-22-08.thinking.2: Compare the mean and the median
y-m-22-08.prereq.0: The meaning of mean (the sum of the scores divided by the number of values)
y-m-22-08.prereq.1: The meaning of median (the middle value when arranged from the smallest)
y-m-22-08.prereq.2: Arranging data in order of size
y-m-22-08.s.s1.prompt: You want to find out whether Mina's statement is 'always' right. What is the most fitting method?
y-m-22-08.s.s1.hint.0: Recall how the mean is determined, and estimate what happens to the mean if one student's score is made very low.
y-m-22-08.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how the other four scores must relate to the mean for all of them to be higher than the mean.
y-m-22-08.s.s1.o.a: Make scores in which as many as 4 students are higher than the mean and test it
y-m-22-08.s.s1.o.b: Calculate just one set of 5 scores and conclude that if it is right in that example, it is always right
y-m-22-08.s.s1.r.b: One example being right cannot show 'always'. What kind of example would you need to find to shake the statement?
y-m-22-08.s.s1.o.c: Believe that the mean is the middle value of the scores, so the numbers of students higher and lower than the mean will be the same
y-m-22-08.s.s1.r.c: You thought the mean and the median are the same. Recall how the two values differ.
y-m-22-08.s.s1.o.d: Say that there are only 5 scores so there's no way to check directly, so you can't know whether it's right
y-m-22-08.s.s1.r.d: You can decide the scores yourself and calculate the mean. Think about what scores you should choose.
y-m-22-08.s.s1.explain: To shake 'always ~', one example that is not so (a counterexample) is enough. Try making scores in which the students higher than the mean are well over half.
y-m-22-08.s.s2.prompt: Write the scores of 5 students from smallest in the order a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d ≤ e, and make 3 different cases in which 4 or more students are higher than the mean.
y-m-22-08.s.s2.hint.0: First set the scores of 4 students similarly high, and calculate how the mean changes as you change the score of the remaining one.
y-m-22-08.s.s2.hint.1: After finding the mean, compare the 5 scores with the mean one by one and count how many are higher.
y-m-22-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Scores must be integers from 0 to 100.

y-m-22-08.s.s2.fail.c3: Fewer than 4 students are higher than the mean. Calculate the mean and count the scores greater than the mean.
y-m-22-08.s.s2.explain: For example, with scores 0, 70, 72, 75, 78, the mean is 59 and 4 students are higher than the mean. 20, 80, 85, 90, 95 (mean 74) or 50, 93, 94, 95, 96 (mean 85.6) also work. When one low score pulls the mean down, all the others can end up above the mean.

y-m-22-08.s.s2.because.model.1: The mean is the value of adding up all the scores and dividing, so if one very low score reduces the sum a lot, the mean can fall below the other scores. For example, because of one student with 20, the mean is 74, and the four students with 80 or more are all higher than the mean.

y-m-22-08.s.s3.prompt: For the same scores of 5 students, up to how many students can have a score higher than the median (the 3rd value when arranged from the smallest) instead of the mean?
y-m-22-08.s.s3.hint.0: Arrange the 5 values from smallest, mark the 3rd value, and point out all the positions that could be greater than it.
y-m-22-08.s.s3.hint.1: Apply the rule that a value equal to the 3rd value is not put on the 'higher' side.
y-m-22-08.s.s3.r.a: Count up to which positions a value greater than the median can be.
y-m-22-08.s.s3.r.b: Think about whether 4 is possible as with the mean, reflecting that the median is the 3rd value.
y-m-22-08.s.s3.r.d: Did you consider that the 3rd value itself equals the median? At which positions are the values greater than the median?
y-m-22-08.s.s3.explain: If you arrange them from the smallest, the median is the 3rd value, so there can be at most 2 values greater than it, the 4th and 5th. Unlike the mean, the median keeps the number of upper data values to half or less.
